Arctic rockling Gaidropsarus argentatus attains a maximum recorded total length of 42 centimeters [Li = 42 centimeters], though some database sources estimate a more conservative 35 centimeters. Field surveys in the Barents Sea indicate that females reach sexual maturity at a considerably smaller size, with the onset of puberty occurring at a total length of approximately 25 centimeters [Lp = approximately 25 centimeters]. This length-based threshold aligns well with the general pattern observed among gadiform fishes from high-latitude environments, where maturation tends to occur at a relatively smaller proportion of the maximum length compared to their temperate counterparts. The observed discrepancy between the ultimate and pubertal length suggests that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth during the early stages of adulthood before allocating resources toward gonadal development.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighed only 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], a minute mass that underscores the substantial maternal investment required to produce a viable clutch despite the tiny size of each offspring. The daily rate is consistent with values predicted for a gadiform of this body size operating at the low end of its thermal tolerance range.

Female Arctic rockling attain an ultimate wet weight of 467.6 grams [Wwi = 467.6 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass reached after several years of sustained growth. At the onset of puberty, which occurs at a total length of 25 centimeters, the corresponding wet weight is approximately 94.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 94.6 grams]. The substantial difference between pubertal and ultimate mass indicates that females continue to add roughly five times their maturational weight after reaching sexual maturity, a pattern that is typical of iteroparous fishes that benefit from increased fecundity with body size. This prolonged post-maturation growth phase allows larger, older females to contribute disproportionately to the annual egg production of the population.

The time since birth at which female Arctic rockling reach puberty has been determined from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Norwegian Sea at a bottom temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. Puberty occurs at approximately 4 years since birth [tp = approximately 4 years since birth], a relatively late age that is characteristic of slow-growing, cold-adapted at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C] marine fishes. The maximum lifespan of this species has been estimated at 10 years since birth [am = 10 years since birth] under similar thermal conditions of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], indicating a life-history strategy that prioritizes longevity and repeated spawning events over early reproduction. This extended lifespan, combined with the significant post-pubertal growth potential, allows females to achieve substantial reproductive output over the course of their lifetime despite the delayed onset of maturity.
